planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous canopy; mulch with leaf litter to mimic native forest floor.

directions: This low, trailing groundcover produces fringed, five-petaled pink flowers in early spring, spreading slowly by rhizomes to carpet the woodland floor beneath deciduous trees. Small bees and early-season butterflies visit the fringed blooms for nectar. Native only to a handful of sites in the Florida panhandle and southwest Georgia and federally listed as endangered, it is occasionally offered by specialty native plant nurseries and makes a conservation-minded addition to a shaded native groundcover planting. Give it consistent moisture and rich, humusy soil rather than heavy clay or dry sites.

planting.note: Best sited in moist, humus-rich alluvial soil at a woodland edge or along a shaded streambank; cold-moist stratify seed before sowing if starting from seed.

directions: A clump-forming native of alluvial woodlands and shaded streambanks, Snowy Campion opens fragrant, star-shaped white flowers in the evening, timed to attract hawkmoths and other nocturnal moths as its main pollinators, with bees also visiting by day. It naturally colonizes flood-scoured riverside woods, so it suits a consistently moist, partly shaded rain garden or streamside planting rather than average dry beds. Populations have declined with the loss of forested river-valley habitat, making garden cultivation a modest conservation contribution as well as an unusual native for shaded wet ground.

planting.note: Propagate by division rather than seed, since seedlings do not reliably retain the dark foliage color; plant in moist, humus-rich soil at a woodland edge.

directions: This selection of the eastern native groundcover emerges with chocolate-purple young foliage that matures to scalloped green, then sends up clusters of bright yellow daisy flowers in early-to-mid spring, an important early nectar and pollen source for mining bees, small carpenter bees, and early-flying butterflies before most other perennials bloom. Like the species, it spreads by rhizomes into a semi-evergreen groundcover suited to moist, shaded woodland edges and stream banks. Discovered as a wild selection in North Carolina, it should be divided rather than grown from seed to keep the dark spring foliage color.

planting.note: Plant in rich, consistently moist soil at a woodland edge or in a part-shade border; divide congested clumps every few years.

directions: This white-flowered form of sweet Joe-Pye weed produces the same domed, fluffy flower clusters as the species but in creamy off-white rather than mauve-pink, held on tall green, not purple-mottled, stems in late summer. Like its purple-flowered kin it is a late-season magnet for swallowtails, monarchs, and a wide range of native bees and other pollinators working the woodland edge. It forms a substantial upright clump best suited to the back of a part-shade border or rain garden with humus-rich, evenly moist soil. The pale flowers offer a useful color contrast where several straight-species and darker-flowered Joe-Pye weeds are already planted together.
